questions.text: Which statement correctly separates approval from sandboxing in this lesson?

options.A: Approval creates operating-system isolation for the approved command.
options.B: A sandbox proves the requested action is desirable and needs no approval.
options.C: Approval authorizes a consequence; sandboxing restricts what executing code can reach.
options.D: A skill’s allowed-tools field automatically provides both controls.

questions.explanation: Approval is an authority decision; isolation limits reachable resources. Neither replaces the other or independently proves correctness.

questions.text: A trusted review skill must run tests from an unfamiliar repository. Which design best bounds repository-controlled code?

options.A: Give it the full parent environment and ask the skill not to read secrets.
options.B: Run it in a scoped disposable executor with restricted egress, no production secrets, and resource limits.
options.C: Approve the test command once and remove filesystem restrictions.
options.D: Rely only on shell=False, since tests cannot launch other code.

questions.explanation: Repository tests can execute arbitrary project code. Isolation, minimal credentials, restricted networking, and bounded resources limit its reach.

questions.text: review_action first checks request.kind=="policy-change" and immediately returns DENY. A policy-change request has approved=True. What happens?

options.A: It is allowed because prior approval overrides the first check.
options.B: It is executed, then the policy is restored afterward.
options.C: It becomes an approval prompt because policy changes are consequential.
options.D: It is denied at the authority-boundary check despite approved=True.

questions.explanation: The unconditional policy-change branch returns DENY before later approval handling. Approval does not bypass this hard boundary.
